title: 16 Comparison of sheep and cattle rumen microbiological responses to an abrupt transition from a high-forage to a high-concentrate diet
content:
Abstract
Sheep and cattle are both ruminant species; however, previous in vitro studies have indicated potential species differences in rumen carbohydrate utilization and acidosis susceptibility. To investigate this in vivo, the objective of this study was to evaluate the response of the rumen microbial community in sheep and cattle when abruptly transitioned from a high-forage to a high-concentrate (HC) diet and subsequent effects on the rumen environment. We hypothesized there would be species differences in response to diet including changes in rumen functional guilds and environmental pH. Individually housed, rumen cannulated Polypay wethers (n=12; initial BW: 60.9±6.11 kg) and Holstein x Angus steers (n=12; initial BW: 485.4±34.93 kg) were blocked by BW and randomly assigned to one of two diets: control (CON; 10:90 concentrate to forage), or high-concentrate (HC; 90:10 concentrate to forage). All animals were first adapted to CON for 14 d, restricted at 2% of BW. On day 1, HC animals were abruptly transitioned to their diet with both diets offered ad libitum, and rumen samples were collected for 72 h. Rumen pH was recorded with a benchtop pH meter at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 h, and rumen functional guilds were enumerated using serial dilution at 0, 2, 4, 8, and 24 h post-feeding daily. Enumeration data were log transformed and all data were analyzed using the PROC MIXED procedure of SAS with repeated measures (v. 9.4, SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC.). Average rumen pH differed by diet (CON: 6.81±0.05, HC: 6.14±0.05; P< 0.01) and by species for the CON diet with sheep (6.75±0.04) having lower overall rumen pH than cattle (6.86±0.04; P=0.02). When animals were abruptly transitioned to a HC diet, regardless of species, lactate-utilizing and amylolytic bacteria proliferated, including amylolytic sub-populations, gram-positive cocci (GPC; Streptococcus bovis and Enterococcus spp.) and Lactobacillus spp. (P< 0.01). Consequently, rumen pH declined (P< 0.01) and cellulolytic bacteria were inhibited (P=0.05). Total amylolytic (P=0.09) and cellulolytic (P=0.06) bacteria tended to be higher in HC sheep than cattle. Regardless of diet, Lactobacillus spp. were greater in cattle (CON: P=0.09; HC: P=0.02), but GPC were more prevalent in sheep (CON: P=0.04; HC: P< 0.01). Additionally, GPC proliferated after HC challenge with populations peaking on d-2 in sheep and d-3 in cattle (P=0.02). Total lactate-utilizing bacteria were greater in CON sheep than cattle (P=0.02), but no species differences were found on the HC diet (P =0.22). These results demonstrate in vivo microbiological differences between sheep and cattle in their response a high-concentrate dietary challenge. Further research is warranted to determine how these variations will impact each species’ rumen physiology and animal performance.
